opus-5.5.text:
I think the core intuition was about generalization. When I started doing research, around 2018 or 2019, computer vision was very successful, but it was mostly successful at specific tasks: classification, detection, segmentation. You train a model for one thing and it does that one thing very well. I kept asking myself what it would take to build a system that could do many things, including things it was never explicitly trained for.

Language seemed special because it isn't just one modality among many. It's the tool humans invented to generalize. We use language to reason, plan, abstract, communicate, and describe almost anything in the world, including images, actions, and math. So if a system could really understand and produce language, it would have access to that whole space of human thought. Vision gives you perception, which is very important, but perception alone doesn't tell you how to reason about a new situation or decide what to do next.

There's also a practical side. Text on the internet is a huge compressed record of human knowledge and human reasoning. Pixels contain a lot of information, but much of it is low-level. Text is already highly abstracted. So the signal you can learn from text, per unit of data, is very rich in terms of reasoning and concepts.

And what really convinced me was thinking about agents. If you want an agent to act in the world, to use tools, browse the web, write code, or interact with people, language becomes the natural interface. You can think in language, act through language, and get feedback in language. That's why a lot of my work, like ReAct, was about letting models reason and act in language. Thinking itself can become a kind of action.

So it wasn't that vision was unimportant. I just felt language was closer to the core of intelligence, the part that lets you generalize. Looking back, I think that bet turned out to be roughly right, though of course now everything is becoming multimodal, and vision is coming back in a different way, built on top of language models.

r001.rationale: The response says language is closer to the core of intelligence and enables generalization, presenting it as central to achieving general AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I started my PhD at Princeton in 2019, vision was the mainstream. That's where most of the talent and compute were going, and I had actually done some vision work as an undergrad at Tsinghua. But I had this nagging feeling that vision, as a field, was about perception, and perception alone doesn't get you to intelligence.

Think about what a vision model does. You give it an image, it tells you there's a cat. That's a mapping. It's useful, but it's a closed loop that terminates immediately. There's no reasoning, no planning, no accumulation of knowledge over time. And crucially, there's no natural interface for the model to act in the world and get feedback. Where does a vision model go after it says "cat"?

Language is different in a few ways that I found very compelling. First, language is the medium in which humans encode almost all of our abstract knowledge. Math, science, law, how to cook an egg, how to negotiate. It's all written down. So if you want a system that absorbs human knowledge, text is where the knowledge lives. Pixels contain the world, but they don't contain our explanations of the world.

Second, and this is the thing I cared most about, language is both an input and an output, and it's an action. When you say something, you change the state of a conversation, or you issue a command, or you query a database. So a language model is naturally an agent. It can read, think, decide, act, observe the result, and think again. That loop is what intelligence looks like to me, and language is the only modality where the loop closes so naturally. That intuition is basically what led to things like ReAct later on, where reasoning traces and actions interleave in the same text stream.

Third, language is compositional and general. A model that understands language can, in principle, be dropped into any task that can be described in words, which is almost every task. Vision models at the time were very task-specific. ImageNet classifier, detector, segmentation model. The generality just wasn't there.

I should say, I wasn't confident this would work as fast as it did. In 2019 the bet looked a bit contrarian. GPT-2 was out, but a lot of people saw it as a toy. What convinced me was less about the models and more about the structure of the problem. If general intelligence means an agent that can learn, reason, and act across many domains, then whatever modality you pick needs to support all three. Language was the only one that did, so I bet on it. I think the last few years have shown that bet was reasonable, and ironically, now vision is being folded into language models rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response says language supports the knowledge, reasoning, and action needed for general intelligence, and that this intuition led Yao to bet on language.

astra-6.text:
For me, the intuition was that language connects to so many different things we associate with intelligence. We use it to describe what we see, but also to express goals, explain causes, make plans, and communicate abstract ideas. So learning language seemed like a way to study many capabilities within a single framework.

Computer vision is very important, but recognizing what is in an image is only one part of intelligence. You still have to ask: What does this mean? What should I do next? Language provides a natural medium for those questions, and it also gives us access to knowledge that people have already expressed in books and conversations.

That doesn’t mean language alone is sufficient for general AI. You still need interaction with the world. But it felt like a particularly promising starting point—a bridge between perception, knowledge, reasoning, and action.

r001.rationale: The response says language connects many capabilities associated with intelligence and calls it a promising starting point and bridge toward general AI.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, language seemed like a more general interface. In computer vision, you might train a model to recognize objects or solve a particular task. But with language, you can describe the task itself, provide context, and express the reasoning needed to solve it—all through the same medium.

Language also connects to so many things people do: communicating, writing code, learning from instructions, making plans. So the appeal wasn’t simply that understanding text was an interesting problem. It was that progress in language could potentially transfer across many different problems.

That doesn’t mean vision is unimportant. But language felt like a promising starting point for building a system that could flexibly understand what you want and figure out how to do it.

r001.rationale: The response presents language as a general interface and a promising starting point for building flexible AI, clearly conveying that Yao saw language as central to general AI.
